Trying to Conceive

Low sperm count: tests, causes and chances of pregnancy

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A low sperm count can make conception harder, but it does not by itself show whether pregnancy is possible or identify the cause. A careful assessment of both partners is more useful than labels such as “weak sperm”. Treatment and timing should match the findings and your family plans.

What low sperm count means

Oligozoospermia means a low sperm concentration in semen. It is different from sperm movement, shape and the total number in an ejaculate. “Weak sperm” is an imprecise label and does not explain the cause or define someone’s worth.

The WHO 2021 lower reference concentration is 16 million sperm per millilitre, not an average or a boundary between fertile and infertile. Mild, moderate and severe labels vary between clinics; concentrations below 5 million/mL often need more detailed assessment. No sperm found after appropriate laboratory examination is azoospermia, not simply the lowest grade of low count.

How it is found and checked

Semen appearance, volume, normal orgasm or previous parenthood cannot establish the current sperm count. Semen analysis measures concentration, total count, movement and shape. Follow the laboratory’s collection instructions and report any lost portion, recent fever or relevant medicines.

Results vary, so an abnormal sample commonly needs confirmation. WHO 2025 suggests repeating outside-reference results after at least 11 weeks; other pathways differ. The clinician sets timing and may expedite assessment for very low or absent sperm. Do not wait months to seek help about a concerning result or symptoms. History, examination and selected blood, urine, genetic or imaging tests look for causes.

Varicocele and infection

A varicocele is enlarged veins around a testicle. It can be associated with impaired sperm production, but is also found in fertile people. Not everyone with low count has one, and a fixed 40% estimate does not predict an individual’s diagnosis. Examination matters; an ultrasound-only finding is not an automatic reason for treatment.

Genital infections, including some bacterial or viral infections and STIs, may affect fertility through inflammation or damage. Not every STI is a virus, and low count alone does not prove infection. Test and treat when indicated; antibiotics are not a universal fertility remedy, and treating an infection does not guarantee recovery of fertility.

Ejaculation difficulties and medicines

Low sperm count can coexist with ordinary ejaculation. With retrograde ejaculation, semen travels into the bladder rather than out through the urethra; little semen or cloudy urine after orgasm can prompt assessment. Diabetes, nerve injury, previous prostate or bladder surgery and obstruction can affect delivery. Tumours or prior cancer treatment may also be relevant.

Some medicines affect ejaculation, hormones or sperm production. Certain blood-pressure medicines, including beta-blockers, can affect ejaculation, but this does not mean every medicine in the class lowers sperm count. Do not assume all antibiotics are harmful. Give the clinician a complete list and review the specific product; do not stop prescribed treatment yourself.

Hormones, genes and targeted evaluation

Brain and testicular hormones regulate sperm production. A hormone disorder may be treatable, but a low count is not proof that taking testosterone will help. Testosterone supplied from outside the body and anabolic steroids can suppress sperm production, sometimes until no sperm are seen.

Very low or absent sperm can warrant specialist assessment for impaired production, obstruction or genetic conditions. Hormone tests and selected chromosome or gene tests depend on the pattern and history; not everyone needs every panel. Genetic counselling can explain implications for treatment and possible inheritance.

Chemicals, metals and heat

Review workplace exposure to pesticides, solvents, cleaning chemicals and heavy metals such as lead. Risk depends on substance, dose and protection, not merely the presence of a household product. Occupational-health advice can help reduce avoidable exposure safely.

Excessive testicular heat may affect sperm production. Consider avoiding repeated high heat and keeping a hot laptop off your lap; comfortable, less restrictive clothing may help. Evidence for each everyday habit and lasting fertility effects is limited. One episode of sitting or wearing tight clothing does not diagnose the cause.

Smoking, substances and body weight

Smoking, heavy alcohol use and some nonmedical drugs are associated with poorer semen measures; evidence for individual substances and pregnancy outcomes varies. Avoid anabolic steroids and cocaine, discuss cannabis and obtain support for tobacco or substance use. Do not abruptly stop prescribed treatment or manage dependence alone.

Higher body weight can be associated with hormone changes and poorer sperm quality, but it is not proof of personal fault or the only cause. Sustainable nutrition, movement and supported weight management may improve health and sometimes semen quality. Neither weight change nor a supplement guarantees pregnancy.

Can natural pregnancy still happen?

Yes, natural conception can occur with low count, though it may take longer or be less likely. The chance depends on the full semen pattern and both partners’ reproductive health, including age, ovulation and whether the tubes are open. A single count cannot provide a reliable personal pregnancy percentage.

Motility describes how sperm move, including forward movement; morphology describes shape. Low concentration may occur alongside movement or shape differences, but they are separate findings. Normal appearance or one normal parameter does not rule out a fertility problem; discuss the combined result.

Intercourse timing and ovulation tests

If comfortable, intercourse every 1–2 days in the fertile window, or every 2–3 days throughout the cycle, can reduce the need to pinpoint one moment. Frequent ejaculation is not automatically harmful to fertility. Follow any separate abstinence instructions for a diagnostic semen sample.

Urine LH tests may help identify the fertile window but do not prove that an egg was released or identify an exact hour; false positives and irregular cycles complicate interpretation. Timing intercourse is not a treatment for severe sperm-production problems. Avoid a schedule that makes sex painful or distressing.

Lubricants and practical self-care

Some lubricants impair sperm movement in laboratory experiments, but this does not prove that every lubricant prevents pregnancy in real life. If lubrication is needed, ask about an appropriate sperm-compatible product rather than avoiding comfortable intercourse or using irritating household remedies.

General health measures can support care, but there is no proven home cure for every low count. Reduce avoidable heat and occupational exposures, seek help to stop smoking, and review alcohol, drugs and medicines. Antioxidants, vitamins and “fertility boosters” have uncertain benefits; do not substitute them for assessment.

Treatment depends on the cause

Options include treating a confirmed infection, addressing ejaculation or obstruction, and selected varicocele repair. Repair is considered for some people with a palpable varicocele, infertility and abnormal semen results; it is not required for every enlarged vein. Discuss benefits, risks, partner factors and the time treatment may take.

Specialists can use targeted hormone treatment for specific disorders; testosterone is not a male-infertility treatment. Assisted conception may include insemination or IVF, sometimes with ICSI, where a sperm is injected into an egg. Very low motile counts can reduce insemination success. Sperm retrieval or donor sperm may be options in selected situations; none guarantees a baby.

When to get help and what to expect

Have both partners assessed rather than waiting for one to finish treatment first. General advice is evaluation after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse, earlier with known problems; age-based earlier referral varies locally, commonly after 6 months when the egg-producing partner is 35 or older. A severe result, absent sperm or planned fertility-affecting cancer treatment deserves earlier specialist discussion.

Seek immediate emergency care for sudden severe testicle pain, or testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicle pain lasting more than one hour or continuing at rest. Do not wait for a fertility appointment. New lumps, swelling, altered testicle shape or concerning discomfort need urgent medical assessment. Low count is not a verdict on parenthood; ask for a clear plan, realistic options and emotional support.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

WHO’s 2021 semen reference values describe a reference population, not a diagnostic fertility boundary. Current EAU guidance supports interpreting the full result and assessing both partners.

WHO’s 2025 guideline suggests at least 11 weeks before repeating outside-reference semen results; pathways and urgent assessment needs differ. AUA/ASRM’s 2024 amendment and current EAU guidance support selected varicocele and genetic evaluation rather than blanket treatment.

ASRM’s 2022 natural-fertility advice distinguishes intercourse timing and laboratory lubricant effects from proven treatment of low count. NHS written low-count guidance was reviewed in 2024 and its testicle-pain page in 2025; these are not newly reviewed 2026 documents.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record results, medicines, cycle observations and questions for both partners’ appointments. It cannot measure sperm, confirm ovulation, diagnose infertility or choose treatment; severe results and urgent symptoms need professional care.

When to seek help

Seek immediate emergency care for sudden severe testicle pain, or testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicle pain lasting more than one hour or continuing at rest. New testicular lumps, swelling or shape changes need urgent assessment. Arrange earlier specialist advice for very low or absent sperm rather than relying on timing tips or supplements.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A reference value is not a fertility verdict; interpret concentration, movement, shape and total count together.
  • Confirm abnormal results and investigate causes with a specialist, sooner for very low or absent sperm.
  • Review medicines without stopping them yourself; testosterone and anabolic steroids can suppress sperm production.
  • Natural conception may remain possible, and treatment or assisted conception depends on both partners’ circumstances.

Frequently asked questions

How is low sperm count diagnosed?

A laboratory semen analysis is needed; appearance or normal ejaculation cannot establish the count. An abnormal result often needs confirmation, with timing and further tests guided by the clinical situation.

Can a varicocele cause a low count?

It can contribute, but many people with a varicocele are fertile. Examination and the whole fertility assessment matter; neither a fixed prevalence estimate nor an ultrasound-only finding means surgery is required.

Can medicines affect sperm or ejaculation?

Some can, depending on the medicine, dose and illness. Certain blood-pressure treatments affect ejaculation; not all antibiotics or medicines in a class reduce sperm count. Ask for a specific review without stopping a prescription yourself.

Can higher body weight play a role?

It can be associated with hormonal and semen changes, but weight alone does not diagnose the cause. Sustainable supported changes may help health; they do not guarantee conception and should not replace other investigations.

Does less than 16 million sperm/mL mean pregnancy is impossible?

No. This WHO 2021 lower reference value is not an average or a fertile–infertile boundary. Consider repeat results, other sperm measures and both partners. No sperm on appropriate testing is a different finding needing specialist assessment.

Should I take testosterone to improve the count?

No. External testosterone can suppress sperm production and cause azoospermia. Discuss fertility plans before hormone treatment; specialists may use different targeted treatments for particular hormone disorders.

Are ovulation kits and avoiding all lubricants a cure?

No. LH kits can guide timing but cannot confirm an exact ovulation time or treat low sperm production. Laboratory lubricant effects do not prove all products prevent pregnancy; seek advice on a sperm-compatible option if needed.

Which symptoms cannot wait?

Seek immediate emergency care for sudden severe testicle pain, or testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicle pain lasting more than one hour or continuing at rest. New lumps, swelling or changes in testicle shape need urgent assessment, not a wait for routine fertility testing.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
